title: Uncomplicated S1 (everything goes right)
v_text: Example Patient A — uncomplicated S1 (everything goes right) Who: Mrs Ayesha Khan, 42, teacher, born 14 March 1984. Why here: three attacks of pain under her right ribs over six months, each after an oily meal, lasting 1–2 hours. Her GP sent her to a surgeon; an ultrasound showed gallstones. She was booked for keyhole gallbladder removal today at 09:00. Scene 1 — Arrival (Step 1) Teacher says: "Okay Ruhan, she has arrived. First, introduce yourself and make sure she's the right person." You ask: "Could you tell me your full name and date of birth?" She says "Ayesha Khan, fourteenth of March 1984." You check the wristband: AYESHA KHAN, 14/03/1984, MR 102938 — matches the notes. You ask about allergies: "None." No allergy band needed. You ask what she's here for: "To have my gallbladder taken out with keyhole." Her husband will take her home and stay overnight. → Identity confirmed. Continue. Scene 2 — Questions (Step 2) What you ask and what she answers - Pain: "Attacks under my right ribs after oily food, settle in an hour or two. None in the last 3 weeks." → typical biliary colic, no current attack. - Red flags: no fever, no yellow eyes, urine normal colour, no back pain. → no sign of complications. - Other illnesses: none. Medicines: none except paracetamol sometimes. Herbal: none. - Previous anaesthetic: caesarean section 2012, no problems. Family: no anaesthetic problems. - Smoking: never. Alcohol: none. - Last food: dinner at 21:00 last night (rice and chicken). Last drink: water at 06:30. Time now: 08:00. → solid food 11 hours ago (≥8 h ✓), clear water 1.5 hours ago… wait — that's less than 2 hours! Teacher says: Good catch moment! Water at 06:30 and surgery at 09:00 means 2.5 hours by the time of anaesthesia — that's fine, because the 2-hour rule applies to the time of anaesthesia, not the time you're asking. Record exact times and let the anaesthetist decide. Pregnancy: you ask privately; last period started 10 days ago, she uses a coil. She agrees to a urine pregnancy test (hospital policy) CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION . Scene 3 — Vital signs (Step 3) Measurement Value Zone Plain meaning Heart rate 76 /min, regular Normal (51–90) Heart beating calmly Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg Normal Good pressure; not high Breathing rate 14 /min Normal (12–20) Breathing calmly Oxygen saturation 98% on room air Normal (96+) Lungs working well Temperature 36.7 °C Normal No fever → no sign of infection Alertness Alert Normal Brain fine Pain 0/10 Normal No current attack BMI 27 (70 kg, 1.61 m) Overweight (South Asian cut-off 23+) Note for anaesthetist; not a problem NEWS2 0 Low Routine observations Scene 4 — Examination (Step 4) Eyes white (no jaundice). Heart and lungs sound normal. Tummy soft; mild tenderness under right ribs only with deep pressure; Murphy's sign negative. Mouth opens well (3 fingers), Mallampati class 2, neck moves normally. STOP-BANG 1. → Fits uncomplicated gallstones; airway looks easy. Scene 5 — Risk (Step 5) ASA 1 (healthy). Clot risk: low (age under 60, no risk factors other than surgery). Anaesthetist agrees: "ASA 1, standard general anaesthetic." Scene 6 — Tests (Step 6) and results (Step 7) Ordered: liver tests (because she has gallstone disease) and urine pregnancy test (policy). Not ordered: chest X-ray, ECG, clotting, kidney tests — she's healthy and under 65, so these wouldn't change anything CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . Test Result Normal What you think Bilirubin 12 µmol/L 3–21 Bile flowing normally ALT 24 U/L ~7–40 Liver cells fine ALP 78 U/L ~30–130 Bile ducts not blocked GGT 22 U/L below 40 (women) Confirms ducts fine Albumin 42 g/L 35–50 Good nutrition Urine pregnancy test Negative — Not pregnant (Ultrasound from clinic) Several stones; wall 2 mm; duct 4 mm wall ≤3 mm; duct ≤6 mm Simple gallstones, duct normal Teacher says: Everything looks acceptable, so we continue. Why? Because: she has the diagnosis we planned for; there's no sign the gallbladder is inflamed (normal temperature, heart rate, no Murphy's sign) or that a stone is in the bile duct (normal liver tests and duct width — 'low risk'); she's healthy (ASA 1); she's fasted; she's not pregnant. Nothing needs fixing or a senior decision. Scene 7 — Treatment/optimisation (Step 8) Nothing to optimise. She needs no regular medicines held. Antibiotic: not needed for a low-risk patient CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . Clot prevention: stockings per local policy CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION . Drip will be placed in the anaesthetic room CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION . Scene 8 — Consent (Step 9) Pain-free, alert, private room, speaks the language of the consultation fluently (no interpreter needed). You explain diagnosis, the keyhole operation, benefits, main risks with numbers, alternatives (watch and wait), and what happens if nothing is done. She asks: "Can I go home today?" — "Most people can, if you're comfortable and eating." Teach-back: "You'll take out my gallbladder through small cuts; there's a small chance of bile leak or needing a bigger cut." ✓ She signs. Scene 9 — Preparation (Step 10) Gown on; wedding ring taped; no dentures; stockings on; temperature 36.7 ✓; pregnancy test documented; consent present; ID band ✓; documents together. Site marking: not applicable (midline operation) CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION . Checklist complete. Scene 10 — Theatre ready, transfer, handover (Steps 11–12) Theatre confirms the keyhole tower, CO2 and spare cylinder, suction, warming and anaesthetic machine check. NEWS2 0 → porter + nurse. SBAR to anaesthetist: "S: Ayesha Khan, 42, for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. B: symptomatic gallstones, otherwise well, no allergies, no regular medicines, previous caesarean without problems. A: obs normal, NEWS2 0, last food 21:00, water 06:30, LFTs normal, pregnancy test negative, ASA 1, airway Mallampati 2, consent signed. R: ready for theatre; no antibiotic indicated per protocol; stockings on." Scene 11 — WHO Sign In (Step 13) Question Answer Patient confirms identity, site, procedure, consent? Yes — she says her name, DOB, 'gallbladder keyhole', consent signed Site marked? Not applicable Anaesthesia machine and medication check complete? Yes Oximeter on and working? Yes, 99% Known allergy? No Difficult airway / aspiration risk? No (fasted, Mallampati 2) Risk of >500 mL blood loss? No Scene 12 — WHO Time Out (Step 14) Team introduces itself. Patient, site, procedure confirmed. Surgeon: 'standard lap chole, about 60 minutes, minimal blood loss.' Anaesthetist: 'no concerns.' Nurse: 'sterility indicators confirmed, tower working.' Antibiotic: 'not applicable.' Imaging: 'ultrasound report displayed.' → READY FOR INCISION. Scenario complete.

title: Abnormal S1: the 'elective' patient who isn't well today (high-risk duct stone)
v_text: Example Patient B — abnormal S1 (the 'elective' patient who isn't well today) Who: Mrs Farzana Ahmed, 61, booked for planned keyhole gallbladder removal. Identity confirmed; allergic to nothing. The clue in the history You ask the red-flag questions. "Have your eyes or skin looked yellow?" — "My daughter said my eyes looked a bit yellow last week. And my urine has been dark like tea." "Any fever or shivering?" — "No." "Pain?" — "Some aching under the ribs on and off." Teacher says: We found a possible abnormality. Yellow eyes and dark urine suggest jaundice — bilirubin backing up into the blood. In a gallstone patient, the most likely cause is a stone that has slipped into the main bile duct. This is NOT what she was booked for. Now check this: look at her eyes, measure vitals, and send liver tests. Measurement Value Zone Plain meaning Heart rate 84 Normal Calm Blood pressure 138/84 Normal Fine Breathing 16 Normal Fine Oxygen 97% Normal Fine Temperature 37.2 °C Normal No fever — so probably no infection in the duct (yet) Eyes Yellow tinge to the whites Abnormal Jaundice confirmed on examination Test Result Normal Zone and meaning Bilirubin 72 µmol/L (4.2 mg/dL) 3–21 HIGH (above 68) — bile is backing up ALP 380 U/L ~30–130 About 3× normal — bile duct cells irritated by blockage GGT 410 U/L below 40 Confirms the ALP is coming from the bile system ALT 160 U/L ~7–40 Moderately raised — liver cells irritated by backed-up bile WBC 9.8 4.0–11.0 Normal — no strong sign of infection CRP 12 below 5 Mildly raised INR 1.1 0.8–1.2 Clotting normal (long blockage could raise it) Lipase 45 below ~60 Pancreas not inflamed Ultrasound today Gallstones; common bile duct 9 mm; no stone seen in duct duct ≤6 mm Duct WIDE — something is blocking it lower down Teacher says: This result makes us more concerned. The pattern is 'cholestatic' — the bile-duct numbers (ALP, GGT, bilirubin) are raised more than the liver-cell number (ALT), and the duct is wide. Using the bile-duct-stone risk tool: bilirubin above 68 µmol/L plus a duct wider than 6 mm = HIGH risk of a stone in the duct CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED (ASGE 2019). Teacher says: Therefore the next step is: do not proceed with today's planned operation. If the surgeon removed the gallbladder today, the stone in the duct would remain and could cause infection (cholangitis) or pancreatitis. Call the senior surgeon. The usual plan is to clear the duct first with ERCP (a camera through the mouth that pulls the stone out), or to image it with MRCP first if the risk were only intermediate — then remove the gallbladder later (local practice CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION ). Explain this to Mrs Ahmed, document, and safety-net: "If you get a fever, shivering or worse pain, come straight back — that could be an infection in the duct." Mrs Ahmed's decision path Jaundice symptoms in history → examine → yellow eyes Fever, shivers, low BP (cholangitis)? EMERGENCY: sepsis bundle + urgent ERCP YES NO Bilirubin above 68 AND duct above 6 mm? HIGH RISK duct stone → postpone today, senior, ERCP pathway YES NO (not reached for Mrs Ahmed) If missed: If the trainee doesn't ask about yellow eyes and doesn't look, the liver tests (if ordered) would still flag it. If the trainee ignores the abnormal results, the senior/anaesthetist character stops the case and the debrief explains: "A stone left in the duct can cause life-threatening infection."

title: the planned patient with an inflamed gallbladder
v_text: Patient S1-E — the planned patient with an inflamed gallbladder What we see: Mrs Rabia, 48. Today: constant pain for 2 days, felt hot overnight. T 38.4, HR 108, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 97%. Murphy's sign positive. WBC 15.2, CRP 96. Ultrasound: wall 6 mm, fluid around gallbladder. How the trainee thinks 1. Fever + fast heart = the body is fighting infection/inflammation. 2. Murphy's positive + right-upper tenderness = local gallbladder inflammation (TG18 group A). 3. Raised WBC and CRP = whole-body inflammation (group B). 4. Ultrasound wall thick + fluid = scan evidence (group C) → definite acute cholecystitis. 5. Grade: WBC 15.2 (not above 18), symptoms under 72 h, no lump, no organ failure → Grade I (mild). 6. Decision: she's not suitable for today's planned list as a routine case — she now has an acute illness. Senior surgeon reviews; antibiotics; she moves to the acute pathway. Early keyhole surgery (often within 72 hours; NICE: within a week) is usually the plan CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . NEWS2 = HR 108 (1) + RR 20 (0) + T 38.4 (1) = 2.

title: high blood pressure
v_text: Patient S1-B — high blood pressure What we see: Mr Tariq, 58, on BP tablets. No GP BP readings in the letter. First reading 172/104. Repeat after 5 minutes rest: 168/102. No headache, chest pain or breathlessness. How the trainee thinks 1. The reading is high (grade 2). Is it real? Repeated properly — yes, still about 168/102. 2. Any symptoms of organ damage? No. 3. Is it 180/110 or more? No. 4. Rule (AAGBI/BHS): below 180/110 in clinic → surgery can proceed. Tell the anaesthetist; ask the GP to review BP after surgery CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . 5. Variant B2: readings 188/114 and 186/112 → postpone and refer for control; do NOT try to drop it rapidly today.

title: diabetes
v_text: Patient S1-C — diabetes What we see: Mrs Nasreen, 55, type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide. HbA1c 58 mmol/mol (2 months ago). Finger-prick sugar 7.8. How the trainee thinks 1. HbA1c 58 is below 69 → diabetes acceptably controlled for planned surgery CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . 2. Sugar 7.8 is inside the target 6–10. 3. Medicine plan: metformin as normal (one meal missed); omit gliclazide today (it could cause low sugar while fasting) CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . 4. Put her first on the list if possible; check sugar at least hourly; tell anaesthetist. → Proceed. 5. Variant C2: HbA1c 82, sugar 13.4, ketones 0.4 → HbA1c above 69 and sugar high → discuss with anaesthetist/diabetes team; usual answer: postpone and optimise CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION .

title: on a blood thinner
v_text: Patient S1-D — on a blood thinner What we see: Mr Imran, 67, atrial fibrillation (irregular heartbeat) on apixaban. Kidney function eGFR 68. How the trainee thinks 1. Ask exactly: "When did you last take apixaban?" 2. (a) "Three days ago, as the pre-op nurse told me." → stopped long enough (needs 1–2 days with good kidneys) → proceed; restart after surgery per surgeon. 3. (b) "This morning — I forgot." → the drug is still active → bleeding risk. The surgeon/anaesthetist usually defer and re-list; reversing a blood thinner is not used simply to make a planned operation possible CLINICAL INTERPRETATION . 4. Pulse irregular but rate 78 → known, controlled AF → fine; ECG to confirm.

title: ate breakfast
v_text: Patient S1-G — ate breakfast What we see: Ms Sana, 39. "I had toast and tea with milk at 07:00." Planned surgery at 09:00. How the trainee thinks 1. Toast + milky tea = light meal (milk counts as food) → needs 6 hours → not safe until 13:00. 2. Tell the anaesthetist immediately and honestly. 3. Likely outcome: moved to the end of the list (after 13:00) or postponed CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED .

title: possible pregnancy
v_text: Patient S1-H — possible pregnancy What we see: Ms Hina, 29. Last period 7 weeks ago. Urine pregnancy test: positive. How the trainee thinks 1. She is pregnant. Planned gallbladder surgery is usually postponed; the senior surgeon, anaesthetist and obstetric team decide. 2. If her gallbladder trouble became urgent during pregnancy, the second trimester is the preferred time for surgery where possible CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED (SAGES). 3. Handle sensitively and privately; she may not have known.

title: the 'high potassium' that wasn't
v_text: Patient S1-J — the 'high potassium' that wasn't What we see: Mr Kamran, 50, well. Potassium 6.4 'haemolysed'. ECG normal. Kidney function normal. Teacher says: "Okay Ruhan, the patient has arrived and he's in a lot of pain. First, the same identity check as always — but quickly." He says "Hamza Ali, 2nd of June 2007"; wristband matches. Allergies: "None." Then: don't make him wait in pain while you do paperwork. Check he's not allergic, and ask the nurse for pain relief now. Pain relief does not hide the diagnosis CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . Scene 2 — First vital signs (Step 3, done early in emergencies) Measurement Value Zone Plain meaning Heart rate 108, regular Fast (91–110) Body stressed — pain? fever? dehydration? infection? Blood pressure 128/76 Normal Circulation coping Breathing 18 Normal OK Oxygen 98% on air Normal Lungs fine Temperature 37.9 °C Normal-high (fever starts at 38.0) Mild inflammation Alertness Alert Normal — Pain 8/10 Severe Needs pain relief now NEWS2 HR 108 → 1; others 0 → total 1 Low Recheck at least every 4–6 h (we'll do more often because of pain/fluids) Teacher says: The heart rate is high. That doesn't mean a heart problem — possible causes are pain, anxiety, fever, dehydration or infection. Everything else is fine, and he's in severe pain. So the likeliest explanation is pain + inflammation. Treat the pain, give fluids, and re-measure. If the heart rate stays high after that, think harder. Scene 3 — First treatment while we work (Step 8 early) What you do in the first 15–30 minutes 1. Drip (cannula) in; take blood at the same time (FBC, CRP, kidneys/salts, group & save per policy). 2. Pain relief: request analgesia: IV paracetamol is a typical first step (SmPC example in Part 8), plus a stronger painkiller titrated by the clinician PATIENT-SPECIFIC DOSE — CLINICIAN CONTROLLED — the clinician prescribes and the nurse administers. 3. Anti-sickness medicine if nauseated (he vomited once). 4. Start IV fluids (he hasn't eaten or drunk properly since last night). 5. Keep him nil by mouth (he may need surgery). 6. Re-check vital signs after treatment. Scene 4 — The history (Step 2), now he's more comfortable "It started around my belly button around 8 last night, then moved down here [lower right] by the morning. I don't want to eat. Sepsis branch YES NO Complicated on scan (perforation, abscess)? Even though the time looks enough, he's an emergency patient in pain who has had strong painkillers, so the anaesthetist still treats him as a possible 'full stomach' and plans RSI CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . Explained: appendicitis; keyhole removal; risks (infection, abscess, bleeding, conversion, bowel injury rare); alternative: antibiotics alone for simple appendicitis — about 7 in 10 avoid surgery at 3 months (CODA: 29% needed surgery by 90 days) but about 4 in 10 have it come back within 5 years (APPAC: 39.1%). Handover to anaesthetist includes: aspiration risk, antibiotic name and time, fluids given, latest NEWS2. Sign In: aspiration risk YES — RSI equipment and suction ready. title: The deteriorating patient (watch the numbers change)
v_text: Example Patient D — the deteriorating patient (watch the numbers change) Who: Mr Usman, 34. Three days of tummy pain he 'tried to sleep off'. Arrives at 14:00. Time HR BP RR SpO2 Temp Alert? NEWS2 What's happening 14:00 102 124/78 20 97% 38.3 A 2 Infection, coping. Workup started. 14:45 (no fluids/antibiotics given yet) 116 112/70 22 96% 38.9 A 5 Something has changed. Heart faster, BP lower, breathing faster, fever higher. 15:15 128 92/58 26 94% 39.2 A 10 Sepsis with poor circulation — EMERGENCY 15:45 if nobody acts 138 82/48 30 91% 39.4 Confused 16 Septic shock — near collapse Teacher says: At 14:45, something has changed. No single number screams 'disaster' yet, but look at the trend: heart rate up 14, BP down 12, breathing up, fever up — all pointing the same way. NEWS2 has jumped from 2 to 5, which means 'urgent review'. A patient with three days of pain, fever and a rising heart rate may have a burst appendix. What the trainee should notice and do at 14:45 1. Notice the trend (the game shows the chart; the nurse may say "His NEWS2 is 5 now"). 2. Go and look at him: sweaty? tummy now tender everywhere and rigid? → suggests perforation with spreading peritonitis. 3. Call for help: urgent senior review (NEWS2 5–6). 4. Start the sepsis bundle: blood cultures, lactate, IV antibiotics, fluid bolus (e.g. 500 mL quickly) and re-check, assess breathing and use oxygen per protocol if below the target range, measure urine. 5. Request urgent imaging (CT) if senior wants it — with a nurse escort and monitor because he's unstable. Results: lactate 3.8 (raised — organs short of oxygen); WBC 19.8; CRP 210; creatinine 142 (kidneys struggling). CT: perforated appendix with free fluid. At 15:15 (NEWS2 10 — emergency) 1. Emergency call: senior surgeon + anaesthetist now; critical-care team aware. 2. ABCDE: airway OK; breathing fast — oxygen; circulation — second drip, more fluid boluses with re-checks, antibiotics if not yet given (NICE NG253: within 1 hour for the high-risk tier), catheter for urine output; disability — alert, check sugar; exposure — rigid tummy. 3. This patient needs the source of infection removed urgently (source control = surgery) once resuscitation has started CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . 4. Consent: if he still has capacity, a brief but complete discussion; if confused, senior follows emergency route CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION . 5. Handover: lactate, fluids given, antibiotic time, NEWS2, kidney injury, aspiration risk. After the correct action BP rises to 108/64 after fluids, HR 112, lactate falls to 2.4 on repeat, urine starts flowing. He goes to theatre urgently. Debrief praises early recognition of the trend. If the trainee fails to act By 15:45 he becomes confused with BP 82/48 (septic shock). Medicines to support BP and intensive care are needed; the debrief shows the timeline: 'sepsis criteria met 14:45; antibiotics given 15:55 (70 minutes late).' If inaction continues, the case ends with a safety debrief.

title: differential diagnosis / diagnostic diversion: it may NOT be appendicitis (ectopic pregnan
v_text: Patient S2-B — differential diagnosis / diagnostic diversion: it may NOT be appendicitis (ectopic pregnancy) What we see: Ms Sadia, 24. Lower-right pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizzy. HR 112, BP 98/60. Last period 7 weeks ago. Urine pregnancy test POSITIVE. Hb 104. How the trainee thinks 1. Positive pregnancy test + tummy pain: ectopic pregnancy must be considered and excluded — a differential diagnosis (a mimic of appendicitis, not a complication of it) CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED (NICE NG126). 2. Shoulder-tip pain = blood in the tummy irritating the diaphragm. 3. Fast heart + lowish BP + low Hb = she may be bleeding inside. 4. STOP the appendicitis pathway. Emergency: call for help, two large drips, crossmatch blood, gynaecology NOW, keep nil by mouth. 5. If the trainee never did the pregnancy test: hard safety failure in the debrief.

title: Diabetes medication error: hypoglycaemia +

Clinical plausibility: Type 2 diabetes and hypertension commonly coexist; patients on several diabetes drugs frequently misunderstand fasting instructions, and taking a sulfonylurea while fasting causes hypoglycaemia (JBDS/CPOC). Why in hospital Planned keyhole gallbladder removal for recurrent biliary colic (ultrasound-confirmed gallstones). Background Type 2 diabetes for 9 years; hypertension for 6 years; BMI 31; ex-smoker. Medicines Metformin, gliclazide (sulfonylurea), dapagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor), amlodipine, ramipril. Allergies None known. Pre-assessment instructions Omit gliclazide on the day; omit dapagliflozin the day before and the day of surgery (UK 2025 consensus); fast from food after midnight; water until 06:30. 2. Initial patient presentation 08:05, day-surgery bay. Mr Siddiqui is sitting on the trolley, slightly pale and sweaty, talking normally but says he feels 'a bit shaky and hungry'. He is fully alert and orientated. Breathing looks comfortable. The nurse has done a first set of observations and a finger-prick glucose because he is diabetic. 3. (includes gliclazide, dapagliflozin, ramipril) - Last food: dinner at 21:00; water at 06:30 - Last HbA1c: "about a year ago" — none in last 3 months - No previous anaesthetic problems; no chest pain; walks 2 km - Symptoms now: sweaty, shaky, hungry 5. First abnormality — hypoglycaemia (glucose 3.6 mmol/L) What the trainee sees Sweaty, shaky patient; glucose meter reads 3.6. What it means Blood sugar below the safe floor of 4.0 mmol/L. Why it matters The brain depends on glucose; untreated hypoglycaemia progresses to confusion, seizures and coma. What could cause it Gliclazide taken while fasting; insulin; alcohol; sepsis. What to verify Repeat finger-prick (clean finger); check symptoms; ask what he took. If confirmed Initiate the hypoglycaemia protocol immediately (he is alert and can swallow, so the protocol's oral fast-acting carbohydrate may apply — in a fasting patient some protocols specify IV glucose; the nurse administers); recheck in 10–15 min. Note: taking glucose by mouth will itself affect fasting — the anaesthetist must know. Who to inform Nurse (now), anaesthetist (fasting and anaesthetic plan), senior surgeon. 6. Second abnormality — SGLT2 inhibitor taken today (euglycaemic DKA risk) What the trainee sees Medication history reveals dapagliflozin taken at 07:00. What it means An SGLT2 inhibitor plus fasting and surgical stress can cause ketoacidosis even when glucose is normal or low (euglycaemic DKA). Why it matters DKA is dangerous and can be missed because the glucose looks 'fine'. What could cause it Instructions not followed. What to verify Check capillary ketones; ask about nausea/abdominal pain; venous blood gas if ketones raised. If confirmed Ketones 0.9 mmol/L (raised, not DKA). The UK 2025 consensus advises omitting SGLT2 inhibitors the day before and the day of surgery, so surgery today is normally deferred; the anaesthetist/senior decide. Who to inform Anaesthetist and senior surgeon. Relationship to the earlier problem(s) Related: both are failures of the diabetes medication plan. Hypoglycaemia (A) plus SGLT2 (B) means starvation ketosis and drug-related ketosis add together — the ketone level must be watched while he is fasting. 7. Third abnormality — no recent HbA1c → result 76 mmol/mol What the trainee sees HbA1c sent (none in last 3 months, NICE NG45/CPOC); result 76 mmol/mol. What it means Average glucose over 2–3 months has been high (above the 69 mmol/mol / 8.5% optimisation threshold). Why it matters Poor control increases infection, wound and cardiovascular complications. What could cause it Undertreated diabetes, adherence. What to verify Confirm no interfering condition (anaemia, haemoglobinopathy). If confirmed Refer for optimisation before rebooking (CPOC). Who to inform Anaesthetist; GP/diabetes team via letter. Relationship to the earlier problem(s) B + C: poor control plus a multi-drug regimen that he could not follow safely → the peri-operative diabetes plan needs redesign, not just a new date. 8. Anaesthetist in the same call What happens next? Repeat 172/100 What changes if confirmed? None today; GP follow-up Decision 4 What do I notice? No HbA1c in 3 months What does it mean? Optimisation status unknown What do I check? Send HbA1c What do I do? (within my role) Await result Who do I tell? — What happens next? 76 mmol/mol What changes if confirmed? Optimise before rebooking Decision 5 What do I notice? Overall picture What does it mean? Medication plan failed + poor control What do I check? — What do I do? (within my role) SBAR to senior + anaesthetist proposing deferral Who do I tell? Senior, anaesthetist What happens next? Team defers surgery; diabetes plan rewritten What changes if confirmed? Rebook after optimisation 10. Unlikely today: SGLT2 inhibitor taken on the day against UK 2025 consensus advice, a hypoglycaemic episode with oral glucose altering fasting, and HbA1c 76; the anaesthetist and senior surgeon decide. (common misses) Usually: the medication history (what was taken today) and the HbA1c timing. What did you recognise correctly?
